Triggers.value: Being in a locked or confined room

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad
I dwell on what I have done wrong
I go over and over the details of the event trying to make sense of it

Threat.value: I feel on guard even inside my own home
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
You can never know who will harm you

vignette: Anaïs Hernandez still recalls the day she was taken hostage by a disgruntled former employee at her company's headquarters. The image of the locked conference room door, the sound of muffled voices outside, and the feeling of helplessness as the hours ticked by are etched in her memory like scars. It was a day that would forever change the way she perceives the world around her. As the days turned into weeks, Anaïs began to notice changes within herself. She would find herself replaying the events of that fateful day over and over in her mind, trying to make sense of what had happened. "If only I had taken a different route to the meeting," she would tell herself, or "Maybe if I had spoken up sooner, things would have turned out differently." This self-blame rumination became an all-consuming habit, making it difficult for her to focus on her work as a project manager. Anaïs also started to experience physical pain in her neck, which would flare up whenever she felt stressed or anxious. She couldn't explain why this was happening, but it only added to her growing sense of unease. Her mind became preoccupied with the fear that she could be trapped again, with no options for escape. This fear of entrapment led her to become increasingly vigilant in her daily life. Even at home, where she should have felt safe, Anaïs would find herself constantly on guard, waiting for something to go wrong. She started to develop magical thinking as a way to cope with the trauma. "It didn't really happen," she would tell herself. "I must have imagined it." But deep down, she knew this wasn't true. The memories of that day were too vivid, too real. This internal conflict only added to her emotional numbness. Anaïs felt like a part of her had died that day in the conference room. She used to be a happy person, but now she couldn't recall what it was like to experience genuine joy. As time passed, Anaïs's behavior began to change in subtle yet significant ways. She started avoiding situations where she might feel trapped or confined. She would take the stairs instead of the elevator, even when her neck pain made every step a struggle. At work, she became increasingly withdrawn, unable to connect with her colleagues on a deeper level. Anaïs's home life also suffered as a result of her trauma. Her divorce from her husband had been finalized a few years prior, but now she found herself isolated and alone. She stopped attending social gatherings or meeting up with friends, fearing that something might happen while she was out. Even in the comfort of her own home, Anaïs felt like she was walking on eggshells, waiting for the other shoe to drop. One day, as she was walking through her living room, Anaïs caught a glimpse of herself in the mirror and barely recognized the person staring back. She looked tired, worn out by the constant fear and anxiety that had taken over her life. In that moment, Anaïs knew she needed help. The weight of her secrets, the false alarms, and the endless analysis of that fateful day were suffocating her. Anaïs's greatest fear is losing herself completely to this trauma. She fears that if she doesn't confront her emotions head-on, she might never find happiness again. As she prepares to seek help from a therapist, Anaïs hopes to learn how to quiet the constant alarms in her mind and rediscover the person she used to be before the hostage situation.
